articleTitle: The importance of IT skills in the employment market
abstract: It has been said before, but I make no apology for saying it again - information technology has already made a significant impact on jobs across all industries. It will continue to do so for many years to come. IT has impacted on every area of working life - from manufacturing, to office administration to retail sales work. The changes which have taken place over the last 10 years or more have brought computers, and their effect, into every aspect of daily life, in particular through the growth of networked systems and access to the Internet. The pace of change over the last decade has been fast and it is likely to continue at an even faster rate over the next decade. IT skills are no longer the preserve of programmers and systems analysts - we all need them

‘One global village,’ said McLuhan. But not according to Hewlett-Packard calculator designers in 1971. They had just introduced the HP-80 Financial Calculator, a business version of the fabled HP-35A hand-held device, and found to their amazement that while the world of science is essentially ‘one-world’, the business world is parochial and fractionated, fraught with specific and local idiomatic convention. Examples include 360-day years in Switzerland, but not in Germany; fixed interest per month in some countries versus daily interest in others; ledgers and calculations of two significant digits in some countries, versus up to 16-digit carry in other countries

articleTitle: ‘How time flies when you's doin' all the talking’
abstract: Since the invention of the typewriter, the keyboard has been king of the human-computer interface, largely because it has been the only one widely available. The search for an alternative method, such as speech, has continued since the 1950s and computers that can be voice controlled have featured in a number of science fiction films, such as the 1968 film ‘2001: A Space Odyssey’. While the conversational skills of the film's master computer HAL have yet to be mastered by today's computers, speech recognition technology has made significant advances from the limited systems that began emerging in the late 1980s. At last speech recognition technology is a viable tool for both business and home computer users

articleTitle: How big is the millennium 2000 problem?
abstract: UK businesses are only slowly waking up to the millennium time bomb. Recent surveys show an alarming level of complacency. Almost 70% of IT Managers either do not realise the seriousness of the problem or have failed to promote the issue in their business. At worst it could bring a business to its knees. Too many think it is a technical matter which can readily be fixed. Very few businesses have even bothered to assess the size of the problem. It should not be treated as just another maintenance and support activity. A full-blown project is required which extends over a considerable time period. The changes will need to be effectively planned and managed. It is vital that firms provide the resources needed in a timely fashion. With 3 years to go time is running out for many

articleTitle: The impact of technology in the twenty-first century
abstract: At AXXIA Systems we spend our working life concentrating on how we can best utilise the latest technological advancements, specifically for the benefit of law firms. Living and breathing computers, and all their ramifications, means that we know exactly how today's innovations will benefit solicitors; by simply putting every source and type of information at their fingertips. Looking forward to the next five years, any member of the AXXIA team could comfortably predict how voice, data and images will all merge on the desktop, into one very easy to use, intelligent system, that will even take accurate dictation, and become the visual gateway to the rest of the firm, family and world. But when I was asked to think about the future and what form technological advancement will take in 15–20 years time, I came to the conclusion that we are heading rapidly, indeed at break-neck speed, towards the end of the industrial revolution

articleTitle: Taking the complexity out of encryption
abstract: The business benefits of electronic commerce and communications are readily identifiable but there is mounting concern over the issue of software security, particularly in the unregulated domains of the Internet and Intranet. The UK's National Computing Centre has estimated that during 1993/94, in Britain alone, over £1.2 billion worth of damage was caused by virus breaches, hackers, data theft and data corruption. MIS Europe, the international consultancy for Computer Security and Data Protection, is launching a new suite of software security products. Developed according to Industry Standard Encryption Algorithms, they are unique in that they provide user-friendly, affordable, ‘off the shelf’ solutions which can easily be adapted to protect, on a global basis, every aspect of a business system. They are equally effective for multinational corporations down to independent users in a single location. The MIS products are multiplatform, and as soon as they are installed, they prevent in-house piracy, prohibit unauthorised external access and provide complete virus protection. Here, the author describes one of these products

Giant awake - Lilliputians sleeping… It is striking to think that while a £3 million a year supercomputer complete with robot and human operator(s) is running all night on the ground floor, the floors above are mostly dark - although there is more disk capacity and MIPS in the building, turned off and silent up there, already purchased by the company, than are running downstairs. So how about shifting the work to the other computers, and getting rid of Madame Mainframe? Sounds like a good idea. But to move in that direction with any chance of ultimate success involves rethinking one's entire viewpoint on client/server architecture. The spectacles we put on to see solutions to other problems could prevent us from seeing the solution to this one
